sections.html:
The Sheriff's counter at 208 S Main St takes the money, and its phone line, (502) 839-4021, answers weekdays from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. The Property Valuation Administrator, reachable at (502) 839-4061, sets the assessment that every bill is built on. Lawrenceburg is the only city, and the small places around it, Alton and McBrayer among them, use the same two offices.

The Sheriff mails bills in the final days of September and starts taking money on October 1. Mortgage companies no longer get mailed copies. A borrower who pays through escrow should ask the servicer in October whether it has the bill.

Owners near the Franklin County line can ask the PVA to confirm which county bills the parcel, since the boundary between the two was changed by a legislative act in 1854.

sections.h2: Discount, penalties and the April 15 cutoff
sections.html:
The Sheriff posts Kentucky's statewide schedule from KRS 134.015 on its tax page. The office accepts cash, checks and money orders only. It won't take installments, and a postmark earns nothing because the money must be in hand on the due date.

Bill stages at the Anderson County Sheriff
StageDatesEffect on the amount
EarlyOctober 1 to November 12 percent discount
Face amountNovember 2 to December 31The printed amount
First penaltyJanuary 1 to 31Five percent on top
Second penaltyFebruary 1 until the office closes April 15Ten percent, plus ten percent more as the Sheriff's fee

From February the Sheriff's add-on is figured on the tax plus the penalty, so the cost of waiting is steeper than the headline 10 percent suggests.

Once April 15 passes, collection moves to the County Clerk and the bill becomes a certificate of delinquency. Added costs are 20 percent for the County Attorney and 10 percent for the Clerk, plus interest of 1 percent monthly. Summer may bring a sale to an outside buyer.

sections.h2: What happens at the clerk's counter
sections.html:
The state revenue agency's model account starts from a $1,000 bill. Once the 10 percent penalty, the Sheriff's add-on and an assumed 4 percent commission are included, it reaches the clerk at $1,254. Paid within five business days it comes to $1,387.79, and after the county attorney's first notice, $1,611.30. Commission rates differ by county, so get a real payoff figure from the clerk.

The first letter goes out within a month of the handoff. KRS 134.128 puts the tax sale between 90 and 135 days after the transfer, with advertising in print and online.

The clerk's website has a delinquent tax lookup named DTax for accounts past April 15. What it shows is informational. The clerk sets the true figure at the moment of any sale, so an owner with an old balance needs a written payoff instead of a screen.

sections.h2: A year in the life of an Anderson County bill
sections.html:
Everything starts on January 1, when value and ownership are locked in. Bills come out in late September, payment opens October 1, and the discount lasts to November 1. After that the printed amount holds through December, penalties step up in January and February, and the Sheriff's part ends April 15.

A spring sale doesn't change the name on that year's bill, which is whoever held title on January 1. How the year gets split between buyer and seller is a closing matter, so ask the agent. Owners who keep the house through the discount window pay least by settling in full before November 1.

Since installments are refused, plan one lump-sum payment. Mailing it close to a deadline is a gamble because a postmark doesn't count. Bring it to the counter on S Main Street, or ask the office how a mailed check is handled.

Appeals follow a set sequence. Every assessment reflects the situation on January 1. The roll is open for 13 days beginning the first Monday of May. A conference with the PVA or a deputy comes first, and the County Clerk takes filings until the next day after inspection closes.

Roughly a month after inspection ends (25 to 35 days), the local appeals board sits for up to five days. Come with documents: descriptions of the land and buildings, insurance coverage, construction costs and comparable listings. A filing with nothing behind it loses. Skipping the hearing ends the appeal, and if the board sets a number higher than yours, a supplemental bill follows.

The PVA takes homestead applications from owners who have turned 65 and from owners classified as totally disabled. For 2025 and 2026 the state subtracts $49,100 from assessed value, a figure that is reset every other year.

Age is shown with a birth certificate, license or passport. A disability claim is renewed yearly unless the owner is a service-connected disabled veteran or has been found permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

sections.h2: Is it worth appealing in a growing county?
sections.html:
An appeal makes sense when the roll shows a number well above what comparable houses nearby have sold for, or when the record describes features your house lacks. It makes less sense when the figure is close and you can't document a difference. Gather evidence first, then decide.

Anderson County had 23,852 residents in 2020, and the estimate for mid-2025 is 25,225. Houses follow people: the county held 10,652 housing units in July 2025, and builders took out 147 permits in 2025. Owners can compare their assessments with recent neighborhood sales before the roll opens.

  • Half of owner-occupied homes were valued above $225,100.
  • Households that own: 77.6 percent of 9,653.
  • Midpoint gross rent: $927.
  • Owners paid a median $1,391 a month with a mortgage and $411 without one.

Before the roll opens in May, pull together two or three recent sales of similar houses on your street and a few photos of anything in poor condition. Showing up with those turns an opinion into evidence, and the PVA can often fix a plain error at the conference without any hearing at all.

Someone who bought last year can list the deed price as next January's value if the home is unchanged.

sections.h2: Clearing back taxes before you sell
sections.html:
1. The Sheriff can quote the live balance, with earlier years included. Past April 15, the Clerk holds that number.
  2. Your closing agent pays arrears from your share and files the release.
  3. The deed needs the buyer's tax bill address (KRS 382.135).
  4. A homestead exemption holder should let the PVA know about the sale.

Behind on taxes and not up for repairs? A written cash offer is one way out. Taxes and clerk charges come out of the price at closing, so the buyer gets a clean title and you keep what remains.

faqs.q: Until what date does the discount last?
faqs.a: It ends on November 1. Anyone who pays the full bill by that day takes 2 percent off under KRS 134.015. From November 2 to December 31 you pay what is printed.

faqs.q: What happens if I wait until February?
faqs.a: From February 1 through April 15 the penalty is 10 percent, and the Sheriff adds a further 10 percent as a fee.

faqs.q: Can I pay in two halves?
faqs.a: No. Partial payments are not taken, and a check that arrives after the cutoff counts as late whatever its postmark.

faqs.q: Where does an objection to my value begin?
faqs.a: Call the PVA and request a conference. The clerk won't take an appeal without it, and the filing window shuts the workday after inspection ends.

faqs.q: How big is the homestead break?
faqs.a: It takes $49,100 off the assessed value for 2025 and 2026, and the PVA handles the paperwork.
